reporting-org.narrative: Yamaan Foundation for Health and Social Development

title.narrative: Voucher Program Mother and Child Health Phase IV

description.narrative: With Kreditanstalt für Wiederaufbau (KfW) funding, the Yamaan Foundation for Health and Social Development (Yamaan) has been implementing a family planning (FP), maternal, and neonatal health services programme in over 200 public health facilities in Lahj, Ibb, and Sana’a Governorates since 2013. The proposed programme will learn from these previous programmes and build on their impact, thereby compounding the positive impact of KfW’s previous investments.Through the proposed Phase IV programme, Yamaan will continue implementation in Ibb and Lahj and expand to AlHudaydah and Aden Governorates to increase access to high-quality contraceptive and safe motherhood (SMH) services through partnership with the public sector (demand-side financing mechanism). The primary beneficiaries will be pregnant women and their new-born babies and women and girls who want to control their fertility. Secondary beneficiaries will be the health facilities, which will have a higher client flow due to increased demand through the voucher programme and will benefit from capacity building and training to provide higher quality services to their clients. This programme will increase uptake of quality SMH and contraceptive services leading to improved sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) of Yemeni women in the target Governorates and strengthen the capacity of health facilities in these locations. In addition, Yamaan will provide extra support to public health facilities that are part of the programme by integrating a performance-based financing (PBF) mechanism to provide additional incentives for providers to strengthen the health system in their locations. By injecting additional income through these facilities (supply-side financing mechanism), they will be supported to provide services more sustainably and make some much needed transformation to infrastructure that has been weakened by long-lasting conflict, and further weakened due to multiple epidemics including, most recently, COVID-19.As a complementary component to Phase IV, Yamaan will ensure we have arrangements in place to continue to provide services during the COVID-19 pandemic, while protecting the wellbeing of our clients and team members. The programme will use a community-based approach to increase awareness of COVID-19 safety measures, and a health system approach to support prevention response and address the shortage of personal protective equipment (PPE) in collaboration with the Ministry of Health (MoH) and the Health Cluster in Yemen which coordinates the response in line with World Health Organisation (WHO) guidelines and standards. Projected service resultsThe programme will distribute 88,123 SMH and 61,686 FP vouchers between December 2020 to August 2022. The total population of the catchment area is 3 million people, of which 284,000 deliveries are anticipated over the 2 and half years of the programme. Through the vouchers, Yamaan expects the programme to support one third of these women – reaching the poorest and most vulnerable women – by providing 88,123 SMH vouchers and 57,280 safe deliveries in Ibb, Lahj, AlHudaydah, and Aden. In addition, 44,062antenatal care (ANC) services will be used through the SMH vouchers. Furthermore, Yamaan expects that the FP and SMH vouchers will support a total of 7,235 women to take up a long-acting or reversible method of contraception (LARC) or a permanent method (PM). Finally, Yamaan will help 25 public healthcare facilities improve the quality of their service delivery through training and the PBF mechanism.

recipient-country.narrative: system is struggling to cope under the pressure of the continuing emergency. More than half of all health facilities are closed due to damage, destruction, or lack of funds. The largest cholera epidemic in the world is currently spreading across Yemen, exacerbated by deteriorating hygiene and sanitation conditions and disruptions to the water supply. 84 percent of Yemen’s estimated 2.9 million internally displaced persons have been displaced for over a year, resulting in additional needs due to depleted savings, lack of access to financial resources and the saturation of available housing capacity. Despite a decline since 1990, maternal mortality ratio (MMR) in Yemen remains among the highest in the region, at 385 deaths per 100,000 live births. The risk is significantly higher for marginalized and vulnerable groups: the MMR in rural areas is 69 percent higher than urban areas, and 80 percent of maternal deaths are among women and girls with less than primary education. The intervening two and a half years of conflict have worsened the situation considerably since these statistics were captured. Women and girls have fewer of the protective factors commonly available to men and boys to mitigate the impact of crisis and emergency: income, assets, access to health and education, social networks, political voice, legal protection and the realization of basic human rights. The incidence of gender-based violence also increases during conflict, with early/forced marriage becoming more common. These factors increase the likelihood of unintended pregnancy and the associated risk. Contraception and safe motherhood services are particularly important under these conditions to enable women to delay and space pregnancies and access vital medical assistance before, during and after childbirth. In 2013, only 45 percent of births were attended by skilled health staff and only 30 percent were in a health facility. 62 percent of women had a need for contraception but only 27 percent were using it. Given the deteriorating health facilities, lack of service providers and essential supplies, it is an even greater challenge for women to access services today. Many women and girls, particularly in rural areas, lack the funds to pay for transport and service costs associated with accessing the formal health system.
